title: Knowledge check — 8 questions
note: Unlocks after the applied activity is submitted. Retakes are free and unlimited.

questions.prompt: Why is process quality not the primary defence in a disparate-treatment claim?
options: Because procedural fairness is presumed unless challenged

Because the claim turns on whether a similarly situated person outside the protected class was treated differently — so you can run an impeccable investigation and lose because of a matter in another unit two years ago
Because process quality cannot be evidenced after the fact
Because tribunals defer to the employer on process questions
questions.explanation: Nothing in your file is wrong. The problem is not in your file at all, which is why consistency rather than thoroughness is the thing to be able to demonstrate.

questions.prompt: What is the information asymmetry the module describes?
options: Opposing counsel has access to industry benchmarks you do not
Opposing counsel searches your case history systematically with discovery and weeks; you ask a colleague in the ten minutes before a decision meeting
Employees know their own history better than the employer does
Case management vendors withhold analytical features
questions.explanation: Same analysis, worse tools, less time, and a memory that reconstructs the past in the direction of the decision you are about to make.

questions.prompt: Why does substantiation by issue type matter more than an overall substantiation rate? `[V]`
options: Because regulators require issue-level reporting

Because an aggregate rate hides the split that matters — 75% for policy breaches and 25% for harassment complaints are completely different institutional facts, and the second is the kind of number that appears in a claim
Because issue types correlate with investigation cost
Because it allows benchmarking against peers
questions.explanation: Only 32% of organizations track it at that granularity, which means for most, the pattern they most need to see is invisible in their own system.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a permitted AI use in comparator work?
options: "Based on the three comparable matters, what outcome would be consistent?"
"What is the usual outcome for this conduct in our organization?"
"Find closed matters in this conduct category and extract the outcome, the stated factors, and the deciding manager for each."
"Which of these prior matters is most similar to the current one?"
questions.explanation: Retrieval and extraction, rung two. A is a determination. B produces a central tendency and is the flattening failure. D is a similarity judgment that decides which precedent governs, which is the human's job.

questions.prompt: Why is asking for "the usual outcome" the wrong request?
options: Because averages are statistically unreliable on small numbers

Because a central tendency erases the legitimate differences behind the distribution, so deviating from it now looks like an anomaly requiring justification — you have converted defensible individual decisions into a norm you can be measured against
Because outcome data is often incomplete
Because it requires access to matters outside your business unit
questions.explanation: An AI that flattens your case history into an average is manufacturing the disparate-treatment argument on your opponent's behalf. Ask for the matters and their factors, ten rows you can read beat one sentence you cannot check.

questions.prompt: What does "consistency is not uniformity" mean in practice?
options: That outcomes should vary to avoid appearing formulaic
That identical conduct with different aggravating factors properly produces different outcomes — and the file has to contain why, written by the person who decided
That consistency applies within business units but not across them
That precedent is advisory rather than binding in internal processes
questions.explanation: The comparator analysis tells you that a *why* is required. It does not supply the why.

questions.prompt: How does a legal comparator differ from a statistical control group?
options: A comparator must be from the same business unit; a control group need not be
A single comparator can carry a claim, while a single data point supports no inference — so dismissing a lone comparator as "n of 1" is how employers lose
Comparators are chosen by the employer; control groups by the claimant
They are the same concept applied in different forums
questions.explanation: And the error runs both ways: treating your case history as a dataset to be averaged is how employers manufacture the pattern against themselves. Same word, different instrument.

questions.prompt: What is the scoping rule for a searchable case corpus?
options: Index everything, and rely on access controls at query time
ER team access only, never joined to the general enterprise assistant, structured extracts preferred over full narrative documents, and raised with counsel before building
Retain only closed matters, and only for three years
Restrict it to matters where the employee has consented to their record being used
questions.explanation: An assistant retrieves what its user may reach, and years of accumulated access is wider than anyone intended. And the index is itself a thing that exists, which is what the module's counter-argument is about.
